"I can hardly believe it's ours," Katherine said, her hand trailing along the cool, painted wood of the window frame. "This view, this little kitchen, all of it. It feels like a story someone else is living."

"Well, you'd better believe it, Kit," Robert answered, setting a precarious stack of plates on the counter with a clatter. "The landlord certainly believes it; I have the signed lease right here to prove it." He grinned at her, wiping a smudge of dust from his cheek. "And are these the gravest worries you can find, that it all feels too good to be true?"

"Oh, you!" she laughed, turning from the window to face him. "You're so terribly sensible. You'd find the practical angle in a fairy tale."

"Somebody has to," he said, enjoying the little shake of the head she gave him. "And you, you're the opposite. You're a poet, through and through. You see a dusty little apartment and call it a castle in the clouds. Sometimes I think you've just invented me, made me up out of whole cloth because you needed a sensible man to keep you from floating away entirely!"

"I am not a poet!" Katherine declared, though she was smiling. "I have to work so hard for my words, they feel as if they're chipped out of stone. But you, Robert, you just seem to know things. You seem to have been born with a plan. When you had to give that presentation to the board, you just squared your shoulders and said, 'Right, let's get this done.' You never seem to doubt for a moment that the pieces will all fit together!"

"Good heavens, I doubt it all the time!" he said, ruffling his own hair in a gesture of amused protest. "I just don't see the use in announcing it to the whole room! You think I'm some sort of grand architect of fate, but I'm not! I'm just a fellow who likes his columns to line up. My father was a bookkeeper, you know. He used to say, 'Robert, a man's life should have a clear ledger, assets on one side, liabilities on the other.' I just tried to keep my liabilities down, that's all. I saved, I worked, I planned for a small, quiet life. Then you came along, and all my careful bookkeeping went right out the window."

"Am I a liability, then?" she asked, her eyes shining with mock seriousness.

"You're the most wonderful, extravagant, unplannable asset a man could ever dream of," he said softly. "I had a column for 'house' and 'career' and 'savings', but I never thought to make one for 'happiness'. You've quite wrecked my system."

"And some people, like my Aunt Carol, seem to have only liabilities on their ledger," Katherine mused, with a little sigh. "They just expect things to go wrong, and so they do. And some, like me," she added, her face brightening, "are born expecting nothing, and are given everything! And we're the truly grateful ones! I shall never make us tea in this kitchen, or watch the snow fall on that street, without a secret little thrill!"

Robert said, "You angel!" and as she turned back to the window, he crossed the small room and put his arms around her from behind. Katherine leaned her head back against his shoulder. "But you are happy, Rob?" she asked. "But I truly am!" he answered. "Why do you always ask as if you expect a different answer?"

"Ah, well, it's because I'm always afraid you'll wake up and realize you've married a daydreamer!" Robert pleaded, using her own word against her. "And I do so want you to be as happy as you've made me!"

"You must have had dozens of sweethearts!" Katherine remarked, looking at their reflection in the darkening glass.

"I never had a single one!" he assured her promptly. "Except for a girl in accounting, as I told you, and she was more interested in my five-year plan than in me, Katherine, and had the nerve to tell me my retirement projections were too conservative!"

"Rob, and what did you say?"

"Sure I agreed with her!" Robert declared. "And then I went right home and bought a ridiculously expensive bottle of wine, just to prove her wrong!"

"Oh, Rob!" and Katherine gave a little laugh that was half a sob, and she turned in his arms to kiss him properly. The sun had set, and the first lights of the city were beginning to glimmer below them, a sprawling, scattered net of diamonds.

"Let's not unpack any more tonight," she whispered. "Let's just sit here and watch the city come alive."

They found two wooden crates that had not yet been emptied, and pulled them to the window. The little room grew dark around them, filled with the smell of old paper from the book boxes and the faint, clean scent of the soap they had bought that afternoon. The sounds of traffic from the street below were muted, a distant river of noise. A tugboat sounded its lonely horn out on the water, a sound so full of melancholy beauty that it made Katherine's heart ache with a joy so sharp it felt like sorrow.

"Was there ever such a night?" said little Katherine. "Shall we ever feel like this again?"

Robert could not see her face clearly in the gloom, but he saw the pale oval of it, the faint gleam of her eyes fixed on the view, the way her hands were clasped in her lap. He put his arm around her, and she rested her head on his shoulder.

"Don't say that, darling!" said Robert. "This is wonderful, of course. But it's only the first page. We have the whole book to live through together. Nothing but the end of the story will ever come between you and me, Kit!"

"And I wouldn't mind the ending," murmured Katherine, staring out at the endless lights. "So long as the story is with you."

Robert could not see her clearly, but he saw the bright, soft glimmer of her eyes in the gloom, the shimmer of her hair where the moonlight touched it, the little blanket-wrapped figure in the middle of the empty floor. He put his arm about her, and she rested her head on his shoulder.

"And I shouldn't be afraid of death," murmured Katherine, staring up at the faraway, indifferent stars. "Strange--strange--strange that we all must go that way some day!" she mused.

"Well, please God," Robert said, his voice thick with a feeling so profound it was almost a prayer, "not for a very, very long time." He drew the wool blanket more tightly around her shoulders. "And not until we've filled this whole apartment with furniture, and books, and laughter. And maybe," he added, his voice dropping to a whisper, "the sound of little feet."

A sweet, sharp pang went through Katherine's heart. She tilted her head back to look at him, at his dear, familiar face, made strange and beautiful by the moonlight. "Oh, Rob," she said. "Is it all right to want so much?"

"It's required," he answered solemnly, and he leaned down and kissed her, a long, slow kiss that tasted of red wine and promises, and the astonishing, breathtaking beginning of a life. The city hummed its endless, sleepless song below them, and in the small, bare room, four storeys up, they had everything in the world.

"I'm just thinking," she said. "About my grandmother. She told me to hold onto goodness. And I was thinking that you're the best person I've ever known."

He looked genuinely taken aback. "Gosh, Julie, I'm not! I'm just an ordinary fellow, as I told you."

Tears, sudden and surprising, pricked her eyes. "Oh, Jim," she whispered. "No one has ever said anything so lovely to me."

He moved from his seat to sit beside her, putting his arm around her shoulders and drawing her close. She rested her head against his chest, hearing the strong, steady beat of his heart beneath her ear. The train sped on through the vast, dark country, carrying them toward their future.

"Well," he said softly, his lips against her hair. "You'd better get used to it. I plan on saying lovely things to you for the next fifty or sixty years."

"Is that a threat or a promise, Doctor Studdiford?" she murmured into his coat.

"It's a diagnosis," he answered. "You're suffering from a severe case of being married to me. And it's incurable."

"It's just as you said," she murmured, turning to Jim. "People are born into this."

"And some push their way in," he reminded her softly, giving her hand a squeeze.

Their suite at the hotel was something out of a dream. It was on a high floor, with windows that looked out over the green expanse of a vast park. The rooms were filled with pale, graceful furniture, bowls of fresh flowers, and a quiet, expensive hush that seemed to absorb the city's roar.

"Jim, it's a palace!" Julia breathed, turning in a slow circle in the center of the sitting room.

"It's all right, I suppose," Jim said, with a comical attempt at a blasé tone. "The last time I was here, they put me in a room overlooking an air shaft. I complained. Apparently they remembered." He tossed his hat onto a chair and began to rummage in his pockets. "Now, where did I put that itinerary? I have a list of things we absolutely must do, compiled by a committee of my most degenerate friends."

"Must we do them?" Julia asked, laughing. She had drifted to the window and was gazing down at the park, where tiny, elegant carriages rolled along winding paths.

"Not a one," he said, coming to stand behind her and wrapping his arms around her waist. He rested his chin on her shoulder. "We can just stay in our palace. For the whole two weeks."

"Could we?" she asked, her voice wistful.

"We could," he said. "But then you'd miss seeing the Brooklyn Bridge, and the Statue of Liberty, and a terribly serious play that everyone says is brilliant, and you wouldn't get to eat oysters at Delmonico's." He kissed her cheek. "And I wouldn't get to show you off."

"Show me off?" she said, turning in his arms to face him. A little shadow of her old anxiety touched her heart. "Jim, I don't have the right clothes for all that. Barbara said--"

"Barbara isn't here," he interrupted gently. "And you, Mrs. Studdiford, look perfect in everything you wear. However," he added, his eyes twinkling, "if it would make you feel better, our first official act as New York residents will be to go and buy you a new hat. The most outrageously expensive, ridiculously fashionable hat in all of Manhattan. How does that sound?"

"It sounds terrifying," Julia confessed, but she was smiling.

"Good!" he declared. "Then it's an adventure!"

The adventure began the next morning. The day was bright and fine, and they walked from the hotel, their arms linked. Julia felt a thrill of pure, unadulterated happiness. Here she was, Julia Page Studdiford, walking down Fifth Avenue with her husband, on her way to buy a hat. It was the sort of sentence she could never have imagined constructing even a few short months ago.

Jim led her to a shop with a discreetly lettered name on the window and a single, perfect hat displayed inside on a velvet stand. A man in a cutaway coat held the door for them, and they stepped from the bright street into a hushed, lavender scented world of pale carpets and soft grey walls. A woman with impossibly blonde hair piled high on her head glided toward them.

"James Studdiford!" the woman purred. "We haven't seen you in an age! And who is this lovely creature?"

"Madame Cecile, may I present my wife, Mrs. Studdiford," Jim said, beaming. "We're on our honeymoon."

"Your wife!" Madame Cecile's eyes, small and sharp, flickered over Julia from head to toe, taking in her simple but well made travelling suit, her new gloves, her hopeful, happy face. "How wonderful! My dear, you have captured the most eligible bachelor in two hemispheres! We had all quite given up on him."

Julia felt a blush rise from the collar of her dress. "It was I who was captured, I assure you," she said, and was obscurely pleased when the woman's painted smile became a little more genuine.

"She needs a hat, Cecile," Jim announced. "Something spectacular."

What followed was, for Julia, an exercise in dreamlike bewilderment. Hat boxes were brought forth. Hats of silk and straw, hats with ribbons, hats with feathers, hats with veils, hats that perched atop the head like bright birds and hats with wide, shady brims were placed upon her head. She sat on a small gilt chair before a three sided mirror, watching her own reflection transform again and again. Jim had settled himself on a nearby settee, offering comments.

"No, too severe," he would say. "My wife is not a severe woman." Or, "That one's jolly! Looks like a fruit salad. Try another."

Finally, Madame Cecile herself brought out a box. Inside, nestled in tissue paper, was a creation of dark blue straw with a wide, sweeping brim, trimmed with nothing more than a single, perfect, cream colored silk rose.

"Ah," said Madame Cecile, with reverence. "This one. It has just arrived from Paris. It was made for you."

She placed it on Julia's head, tilting it to just the right angle. Julia stared at the woman in the mirror. It was not the girl from Sausalito, nor the shy bride, nor even the happy young wife on the train. The woman in the mirror was poised, elegant, a stranger. A woman who belonged in this shop, on this street, in this city. A woman of the world.

"Oh," Julia whispered. It was beautiful. It was also, she knew with a sinking certainty, more expensive than anything she had ever owned in her life.

"We'll take it!" Jim said triumphantly from the settee. "It's perfect!"

"Jim, we can't," Julia said in a low voice, turning to him. She felt the blood drain from her face. "Jim, no, really."

"What do you mean, we can't?" he asked, his face a picture of confusion. "Of course we can. It looks stunning on you, Ju. You look like a queen."

"A queen who is about to be bankrupt," she tried to joke, but her voice trembled. She looked at Madame Cecile, who was watching them with polite, professional interest. "May we have a moment?" she asked.

The woman, with a slight, knowing inclination of her head, glided away.

"Darling, what is it?" Jim asked, coming over to her chair. He knelt beside her, taking her hand. "Don't you like it? I thought you loved it."

"I do love it," she whispered, her eyes filling with tears. "It's the most beautiful hat I've ever seen. That's the problem. Jim, I can't let you buy it. I saw the price tag when she took it out of the box." She swallowed hard. "It costs seventy-five dollars."

Jim looked at her, his brow furrowed. "Well, yes," he said slowly. "It's from Paris. I imagine it would be dear. What of it?"

"What of it?" she repeated, her voice rising in a sort of desperate incredulity. "Jim, my grandmother's pension, the one she lived on for a whole year, was two hundred dollars. This is a hat! For seventy-five dollars! It's... it's a sin."

"Oh, dearest," he said, and the rueful, loving look was back on his face, the one he had worn when she'd first called him young. "It's not a sin. It's just a hat. It's money, that's all. And we have it."

"But that's just it!" she cried, pulling her hand away. "You have it! I don't! I feel like... like a charity case. Like a little girl you've taken to a sweet shop. I can't just let you buy me seventy-five-dollar hats as if it were nothing!" She looked down at her hands, twisting her new rings. "I'm not used to it. It doesn't feel right. It makes me feel... small."

James Studdiford was, as Julia had observed, a man to whom things came easily. He was not accustomed to problems that could not be fixed with a confident hand, a bit of luck, and a cheerful assumption that all would be well. But he was also a man deeply in love, and he could see past the tears and the trembling voice to the real pain in his wife's heart. He was beginning to understand that the chasm between the 'bad belt' and the 'good belt' was not just a matter of money, but a deep and winding canyon of experience and feeling that he had never had to cross.

He stood up and walked over to Madame Cecile. Julia, watching him, her heart hammering, expected him to pay for the hat, to override her objections with a kind but firm hand. It was what she would have expected of any man of his class.

"Madame," Jim said, his voice quiet but clear. "My wife and I are grateful for your time. The hat is indeed exquisite, but she feels it is not quite right for her. We will have to continue our search elsewhere."

Madame Cecile's eyebrows shot up into her improbable hair, but she was a professional. "Of course, Doctor Studdiford," she said smoothly. "Perhaps another time."

Jim came back to Julia, held out his hand, and pulled her to her feet. "Come on, you angel," he said, his voice full of a warmth that had nothing to do with money. He led her out of the shop, past the bowing doorman, and back into the bright, noisy sunlight of Fifth Avenue.

They walked for a full block in silence. Julia's mind was reeling. He had listened. He had understood. He had not dismissed her feelings or patronized her or bought the hat anyway. He had sided with her, against the expectations of his world.

"Thank you," she said finally, her voice thick.

"For what?" he asked, tucking her arm more securely in his.

"For not buying the hat."

"Oh, that," he said, as if it were nothing. "Well, to be perfectly honest, Ju, I thought the one with the fruit salad was much more your style."

She stopped in the middle of the pavement and looked up at him, and saw in his eyes not just love, but a dawning comprehension, a willingness to learn a language he had never needed to speak. And she began to laugh, a real Julia laugh, a gale of laughter right there on Fifth Avenue.

"Oh, Jim!" she said, wiping her eyes. "You are the most ridiculous, wonderful man in the world!"

"I know," he said, looking immensely pleased with himself. "Now, I'm starving. My expert committee strongly recommends a place around the corner that serves luncheon. They have sandwiches that don't cost seventy-five dollars. I've checked."

As he led her away, Julia felt a profound shift inside her. She was still Julia Page Studdiford, and she was still on her honeymoon in a city of impossible grandeur. But she was not alone in a foreign land. She was with Jim. And she was beginning to see that pushing into the good belt was not about learning to spend money without a thought; it was about learning to build a life together, a life that had room for both the boy who was born lucky and the girl who had to learn things so hard they dug right down into the very soul of her. And that, she thought, was the luckiest thing of all. They were not two separate people, one from the good belt and one from the bad. They were making a new place, all their own.
